title: O Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 19:1)
hook: the king weeps for the son who rebelled: "would I had died for thee"
carry: would I had died for thee
tomorrow: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)

segments.voice: Yesterday Shimei threw stones from the ridge, and David kept walking. Your line was one choice, on one road, to keep walking. Today, the war with Absalom ends, and the news reaches his father.
screen: `ONE CHOICE, ON ONE ROAD, TO KEEP WALKING.`

segments.voice: Before the battle, the king stands at the gate as his army marches out, and gives one order, loud enough for every soldier to hear: deal gently, for my sake, with the young man, with Absalom. The fighting is in the forest of Ephraim, and the forest, the text says, devours more people than the sword. A watchman on the wall sees a runner. Then another. David has one question for each of them, and it isn't about the battle. Is the young man Absalom safe?
screen: `DEAL GENTLY WITH THE YOUNG MAN.` → `THE FOREST OF EPHRAIM.` → `IS ABSALOM SAFE?`

segments.voice: He wasn't. Riding a mule under a great oak, Absalom caught his head fast in the tree, and the mule went on, leaving him hanging between heaven and earth. A soldier saw him and wouldn't touch him, because of the king's order. Joab didn't hesitate. Absalom died there, and they threw him into a pit in the forest and heaped stones over him. The second runner, a Cushite, answers the king in the gentlest words he can find: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. David understands. He is shaken, and goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, and as he goes he says: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! "would I had died for thee", O Absalom, my son, my son! Over Saul and Jonathan, David made a song. Here there is no song, only broken words circling back to one: my son. This is the son who stole the people's hearts, drove his father barefoot out of the city, and came after his life. David's grief has no conditions. He doesn't say, if only he hadn't rebelled. He wishes he had died in his place. It doesn't stay private. The victory turns to mourning, and soldiers slip back into the city like people ashamed after a defeat. Joab tells the king bluntly he is shaming the men who saved his life. And David gets up and sits in the gate. A father's grief that holds nothing back, and a king who still has to face his people.
screen: `CAUGHT IN THE OAK.` · `THE RUNNER'S GENTLE NEWS.` · then, large: `WOULD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.` · then: `MY SON, MY SON.` · `THE KING SITS IN THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a loss you've told yourself you shouldn't feel so much, like someone who walked away. If your grief keeps adding a but, they chose it, but, I should be over it, but, drop the but for a few breaths and let yourself miss what you miss. If you pray, you can remember them before God by name.
O Absalom. A father's cry over the son who rebelled against him, my son, my son, wishing he had died instead. Today's word.
Your line: would I had died for thee. Grief with no conditions on it. That's day seven hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Jews read David's lament for Absalom as part of the book of Samuel; in Jewish Bibles the cry is the opening verse of chapter 19, while English Bibles that follow the King James numbering place it at the end of chapter 18.

chat.says: Absalom tried to take his father's throne. Why did David grieve him so much?
options: He was still his son; David wished he'd died in his place, no conditions.
He grieved only because the battle cost him so many soldiers.
He had ordered Absalom's death and felt guilty about giving it.
chat.meaning: David cried, O my son Absalom, would I had died for thee: grief with no conditions for the son who sought his life.

Ephraim.meaning: the forest where the battle was fought

Cushite.meaning: a man from Cush, the second runner

Absalom.meaning: David's son, who rose against him
